Journal.Title: International journal of sports physiology and performance

Article.ArticleTitle: RPE During Concentric and Eccentric Cycling: Are We Measuring Effort or Exertion?

Abstract.AbstractText: Despite the terms often being used interchangeably it has been suggested that perceptions of effort and perceptions of exertion may differ. Eccentric cycling may provide a model of exercise by which differences between these perceptions can be examined.
of this study was to examine and compare perceptions of effort and exertion during eccentric and concentric cycling at four intensities.

Ten healthy male participants (mean ± SD; age: 29.8 ± 2.3 y) performed an incremental cycling test for the determination of maximal aerobic power output (MAP), followed in a randomized and crossover design, by four 5-min bouts (30%, 60%, 80% and maximal) of either eccentric (ECC) or concentric (CONC) cycling. Through each bout participants were asked to report their perceived effort, exertion and muscle pain. Heart rate (HR) and oxygen consumption (VO2) were continuously recorded throughout each bout.

Perceived exertion was greater for CONC at 30% (8.5 ± 1.5 vs. 7.1 ± 1.8; P=0.01), 60% (12.4 ± 1.4 vs. 10.3 ± 2.0; P=0.01), 80% (15.8 ± 1.7 vs. 12.4 ± 2.5; P<0.01) and MAX (17.2 ± 1.3 vs. 15.6 ± 1.8; P=0.03) in comparison to ECC. Perceptions of effort and pain were similar between CONC and ECC. HR and VO2 were greater during CONC than ECC.

Perceived exertion was greater during concentric compared with eccentric cycling, yet effort was similar between conditions despite different physiological stress. Such findings have implications for understanding the development of such perceptions during exercise.
